newsitem.title: ITALY: Appeals grow in Italy to spare U.S. death row man.
newsitem.headline: Appeals grow in Italy to spare U.S. death row man.

text.p: The Italian parliament, lawyers and the country's Red Cross joined calls on Monday for a campaign to halt the execution on Wednesday of a prisoner in the United States who says he can prove his innocence.

Italy's lower house of parliament voted by 399 to three, with 13 abstentions, in support of a resolution urging the Italian government to intervene on behalf of Joseph O'Dell, echoing a similar call last week in the upper Senate.
O'Dell, 55, is due to die by lethal injection in Virginia on December 18 unless the U.S. Supreme Court stays his execution or state governor George Allen accepts a clemency plea.

O'Dell was convicted in 1985 of the murder of a 44-year-old woman, secretary Helen Schartner. His supporters say DNA testing proves he did not carry out the crime but that judges have refused to admit the evidence on a legal technicality.

The case has shocked Italy, where there is strong support for a worldwide ban on capital punishment, and prompted a personal plea from Pope John Paul to the U.S. federal government as well as to the state of Virginia to spare O'Dell.
The Italian Red Cross on Monday published two telefax numbers for Allen's office and urged the public to bombard him with pleas for clemency.

"The idea that a person who is not guilty can be killed because of a law is repugnant and an offence to civilised society," the acting head of the national Red Cross, Maria Pia Garavaglia, said in a statement.
The chairman of the Italian criminal lawyers' association, Gaetano Pecorella, called for a one-hour halt to all court cases in Italy if O'Dell's execution proceeds.

"On December 18, the state of Virginia will kill a man. We are asking all lawyers to unite against the death penalty and against all forms of torture and violation of human rights," he wrote in a letter to other Italian legal associations.
O'Dell, who represented himself at his first trial, claims post-judgment DNA testing of blood found on his clothing shows it does not match that of the victim.

Supporters, who have been campaigning for O'Dell over the Internet, say a court of appeal refused to admit the evidence because O'Dell did not raise the proper objections that would have allowed him to preserve certain issues for appeal.
If no objection is made to an issue during trial, the issue cannot be appealed.
